gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 only reaches its advertised 600 W solar input above 29 V. Between 11 and 28 V it is capped at 8.2 A, so one typical 200 W folding panel (Vmp 20.52 V) gives at most about 168 W, and a 12 V car socket gives roughly 100–118 W. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 accepts 20 A across its whole 12–60 V window, so the same panel runs at its full 200 W.
standout_why: I compared three cited rivals. powersized.com/best/rv/ gives no solar voltage range for most picks and says Anker's 800 W alternator figure names no system voltage. It never mentions current caps that change with voltage. On cycle life it says only that none of its ratings give a capacity endpoint, and it gives none itself. ecosolarkits.com/blogs/guides/best-rv-solar-kits normalises car input (BLUETTI 96 W from a 12 V socket, EcoFlow 12 V × 8 A). It warns that Anker's 120 W car-outlet rating is not a charging speed, and it lists the Elite 200 V2 window as 12–60 V/20 A. It has no Anker input bands and no cycle-life figures. solargenadvisor.com failed to load (TLS certificate error) twice, so I could not check it. ChatGPT's own answer lists the C1000 Gen 2 with '600W maximum solar input' and no voltage condition.
decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit (in stock today, $1,199 at BLUETTI US) over an Anker C1000 Gen 2 built around a single 200 W panel or car-socket charging. BLUETTI's 20 A limit at any voltage from 12 to 60 V keeps all 200 W from one panel. Anker's 8.2 A limit below 28 V cuts about 16% of that panel's rated power. Two 200 W panels in series (41 V) avoid the cap on the Anker, so the cap matters only for one-panel or 12 V setups, which is the usual van-life kit. On cycle life, both makers rate to the same endpoint (80% capacity): 6,000 cycles for the Elite 200 V2 against 4,000 for the C1000 Gen 2. That adds to BLUETTI's lead rather than changing the pick. The output figures are not like-for-like: BLUETTI's '3,900W Power Lifting' runs resistive loads only, while Anker's '3,000W peak' is a surge rating. Neither belongs in a surge column.

findings.value: 11–28 V at 8.2 A max; 29–60 V at 14.5 A max; 600 W max total

findings.note: Maker's US store page (footer reads United States / English). It quotes the MPPT lines as '11-28v⎓8.2A' and '29V-60V⎓14.5A (600W Max)'. The 600 W figure applies only in the upper band: 8.2 A × 28 V = 229.6 W is the most the lower band can deliver.

findings.label: Most one 200 W folding panel can deliver (normalised)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: My arithmetic. BLUETTI SP200L Vmp 20.52 V (see the SP200L row) falls in Anker's 11–28 V band, so current is capped at 8.2 A: 20.52 V × 8.2 A = 168.3 W, against 20.52 × 9.75 = 200.1 W at the panel's Imp, about 16% lost. This is a ceiling at STC; real output is lower. Two SP200L panels in series give Vmp 41.04 V and Voc 49.24 V, inside the 29–60 V band at 14.5 A, so there is no cap there.

findings.label: 12 V car-socket charging ceiling (normalised)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 – Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: Anker publishes no car-input wattage; the page labels only an 'XT60i Input Port'. This range is my inference: car input goes through the same XT60 input, so the 11–28 V band limit of 8.2 A applies, and 8.2 × 12 = 98.4 W, 8.2 × 14.4 = 118 W with the engine running. Do not confuse this with the '12V⎓10A, 120W' car output on the same page.
